title: Insurance Basics
summary: Match your household’s risks to your policies, find the gaps and get ready for a claim.
subtitle: Translate the policy before asking it to protect the household

blocks.text: Insurance is a contract for sharing financial risk, written in a dialect that occasionally appears to charge by the syllable.

This lesson will not choose a product, insurer or coverage amount for you. It will help you find the losses your household could not easily absorb. It will also help you decode policy terms, compare quotes on equal coverage and get ready for a claim or complaint. The policy sets the real terms, not the ad or a friendly summary.

Insurance does not stop the emergency from happening. It decides which covered losses get paid, up to what limit and after what deductible. It also depends on the exclusions, conditions and evidence you provide.

items.title: “Insurance covers anything bad that happens.”
items.text: A policy covers set events, property, people and amounts, within its exclusions, deductibles, limits and conditions. Maintenance, wear and some hazards may be excluded or need an endorsement.

blocks.text: Two quotes $18 apart can protect two very different households.
blocks.detail: Reading the same six terms in every quote turns a confusing price gap into an honest comparison.
blocks.extra: Decode the six terms next, before a single quote gets compared.

sections.title: Six Terms That Control the Outcome

blocks.text: Compare quotes using the same property, limits, deductibles, endorsements and assumptions. A lower premium can mean a real saving, a bigger share of the risk falling on you, less coverage, or some mix of all three. Ask for the differences in writing.

items.title: Premium
items.text: The amount charged for coverage.

items.title: Deductible
items.text: The amount you pay toward a covered claim before the insurer pays the rest.

items.title: Coverage limit
items.text: The most the insurer will pay under that coverage.

items.title: Exclusion
items.text: A loss, cause, person, property or situation the policy does not cover.

items.title: Endorsement
items.text: A written change to the policy.

items.title: Settlement basis
items.text: Replacement cost and actual cash value can mean different payouts.

blocks.text: Example: Policy A costs $1,560 a year with a $500 deductible. Policy B costs $1,320 with a $1,500 deductible. B saves $240 a year, but it hands the household $1,000 more in upfront claim cost.

items.title: “The cheapest premium is the cheapest policy overall.”
items.text: Price is only one layer. Compare limits, deductibles, exclusions, endorsements, settlement basis, service and how much of the loss lands back on your household.

sections.title: Nina and the Quote That Won by $18

paragraphs: Nina Patel moves from a rented Ottawa apartment into a small townhouse. Her old tenant policy was easy to ignore, which is a sentence insurance policies hear just before they become important. She gets two home-policy quotes. One is $18 cheaper each month. The decision looks finished.

Then Nina’s brother asks if both quotes cover the same things. They don’t. The cheaper quote has a higher deductible, a lower limit for valuables and no sewer-backup endorsement. One quote pays replacement cost for listed items. The other is unclear. Nina isn’t sure which differences matter. The price is doing an excellent job of distracting everyone.

Nina makes a room-by-room inventory with photos, model numbers and receipts. She lists the risks she could not cover alone: liability, a big loss of belongings and a place to stay if she has to leave home. Then she sends each licensed agent the same written questions. They cover limits, deductibles, exclusions, water damage, payout basis, endorsements and claims service. ‘Show me how each contract responds to these risks.’

The answers show that the cheaper price partly comes from leaving more risk with Nina. She picks the contract whose written terms fit her needs, puts the deductible in her emergency fund and stores the policy, inventory and claims number away from the home.

Months later, a supply line bursts and ruins her flooring and some belongings. Nina shuts off the water safely, protects the area, takes photos and calls the insurer. She keeps her receipts and holds on to the damaged items until she is told what to do. The claim takes patience and proof. But she does not have to rebuild her household from memory. She compared the risk, not the loudest price.

blocks.text: An inventory helps with coverage planning and with a claim. Keep a copy of the photos, receipts, serial numbers and the policy somewhere you can reach even if your home or device is not.
Nina turned two different quotes into one fair comparison. She made her choice on purpose, set money aside for the deductible and got her evidence ready before a loss ever happened.
A burst pipe found Nina ready, because she built her evidence file months before she needed it.
blocks.detail: Turning a loss into a calm checklist instead of a scramble is what let Nina's claim move on proof instead of memory.
blocks.extra: Build your own coverage-gap map next, before anything goes wrong.

items.title: Protect people first
items.text: Call emergency services when needed, and prevent further damage only when it is safe to do so.

items.title: Notify promptly
items.text: Check the policy’s steps and deadline, then contact the insurer or your representative as soon as you can.

items.title: Document carefully
items.text: Photograph the damage, list the items, keep receipts and write down your conversations. Ask before repairing or throwing anything out, except for urgent safety steps.

items.title: Escalate in order
items.text: Use the insurer’s own complaint process and ask for its final decision. If the problem is still not resolved, you may take it to the right ombudservice or provincial regulator.

blocks.text: Water damage is not one single coverage. Flood, sewer backup, overland water, a burst pipe and normal wear can each be treated differently. Read the definitions and exclusions, and ask if an endorsement is available.

items.title: “If a claim is denied, there is nothing I can do.”
items.text: Ask for the decision and the reason in writing. Send any missing evidence. Use the insurer’s complaint process. If you still disagree, turn to the right ombudservice, regulator or legal advice.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: How is a premium different from coverage?
items.detail: The premium is the price you pay. Coverage is the protection the policy’s terms, limits and conditions give you.

items.title: What trade-off can accompany a higher deductible?
items.detail: A lower premium may shift more of the upfront claim cost onto the household.

items.title: How does an exclusion differ from an endorsement?
items.detail: An exclusion removes coverage for something specific. An endorsement is a written change to the policy.

items.title: Why compare two quotes on like-for-like terms?
items.detail: Different terms can mean the two prices are buying different protection.

items.title: What should happen first after a loss, and what evidence should be preserved?
items.detail: Protect people first. Prevent more damage only when it is safe. Tell the insurer promptly and keep photos, lists, receipts, damaged items and notes on every call.

blocks.text: Agents and brokers must be licensed where they operate. Regulators can confirm a licence and explain the complaint routes, but they will not rewrite the policy after a loss.

Use this page to prepare questions, not to make a personal coverage decision. Record where policies are kept and general contacts, but leave out passwords, full ID numbers or sensitive medical details.

Review coverage after a move, a renovation or a big purchase. Review it again after a new driver, business use, a relationship change or an income change. A policy can stay active while going out of date with remarkable professionalism.
Compare the risk transfer, not the loudest price.
blocks.detail: Read the policy terms. Compare quotes on equal coverage. Save the deductible. Get your evidence and claim steps ready before the household needs them.

items.title: Premium
items.text: The amount charged for insurance coverage.

items.title: Deductible
items.text: The amount you pay toward an eligible claim before the insurer pays the rest.

items.title: Coverage limit
items.text: The most the insurer will pay under a particular coverage.

items.title: Exclusion
items.text: A loss, cause, person, property or situation the policy does not cover.

items.title: Endorsement
items.text: A written change to the policy.

items.title: Actual cash value
items.text: A payout that generally reflects an item’s value after wear and age, based on the policy wording.

items.title: Replacement cost
items.text: A payout basis that pays to replace covered property, within the policy’s rules and limits.

quiz.question: True or False: “Insurance covers anything bad that happens.”

questions: Which people, property, income or risks could your household not easily replace?
Which policies and workplace or card benefits do you already have?
For one policy, what are the premium, deductible, key limits and settlement basis?
Do you have your deductible saved? What would a loss leave for you to cover?
What is one exclusion, condition or endorsement you need explained in writing, and when will you review your coverage?
